After: the self-loop is gone, shown dashed, while both parallel C to D edges remain." width="100%"} A self-loop is an edge where the source and target nodes are the same. This method removes all such edges from the graph, which is a common preprocessing step for many graph algorithms that assume simple graphs. Self-loops often appear as artifacts of data collection (a user replying to their own post, a page linking to itself, a gene interacting with itself) and can distort degree counts, clustering coefficients, and similar metrics. Every self-loop is removed, including multiple loops on the same node, while all nodes are kept. The graph is modified in place; if any loops were removed, the change is recorded as a single step in the step log (see `steps`). On a graph without self-loops the call does nothing. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The removal works uniformly for directed and undirected graphs and touches only self-loops (edges of the form $(v, v)$), so parallel edges between distinct endpoints are left in place. If your goal is a fully simple graph, chain this with `remove_duplicate_edges()` or call `simplify()` in one step. To inspect what you're about to lose first, `which_loops()` returns the offending edge IDs and `count_loops()` gives their per-node totals. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A self-loop connects a node to itself; here two of the three edges are self-loops on "A" and "B", which `which_loops()` reports by edge ID: ::: {#520bfc15 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "A"), # self-loop ("B", "B"), # self-loop ] ) ) g.count_edges(), g.which_loops() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (3, [2, 3]) ``` ::: ::: Calling `remove_selfloops()` strips both self-loops, leaving only the genuine connection between the two nodes: ::: {#872341b9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.remove_selfloops() g.count_edges(), g.which_loops() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1, []) ``` ::: ::: This is a common cleanup step before algorithms that assume a simple graph. As long as no multi-edges remain, `is_simple()` now returns `True`: ::: {#bc603dc4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["X", "Y", "Z"]) .add_edges( [ ("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z"), ("X", "X"), # self-loop ] ) .remove_selfloops() ) g.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Parallel edges between different nodes are not affected. Here the duplicated X-Y edge survives, so the graph is still not simple; `simplify()` would remove both kinds: ::: {#650e9a1c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["X", "Y"]) .add_edges( [ ("X", "Y"), ("X", "Y"), # parallel edge ("Y", "Y"), # self-loop ] ) .remove_selfloops() ) g.count_edges(), g.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (2, False) ``` ::: :::
